sources.title: The prairie traveler. A hand-book for overland expeditions (Randolph B. Marcy), Harper & Brothers, 1861 printing
sources.publisher: Library of Congress (Joseph Meredith Toner Collection, digitized book)
sources.supports: Digitized public-domain handbook by Capt. Randolph B. Marcy, U.S. Army, 'published by authority of the War Department'. Contents list (seven chapters, read in full) shows chapters on routes, wagons and teams, stores and provisions (including anti-scorbutics), camp life including fuel and making fires, and guides. Preface says it draws on the author's frontier experience and on officers' reports for the routes.
sources.notes: Upgraded from the register placeholder. The drafting agent read the LOC catalogue record and the OCR snippets of the first 25 of 398 page images (title page, copyright page, preface, both contents pages and the opening of chapter I). The two contents pages (images 17 and 18) were read in full on 2026-11-01; the book's full-text file could not be fetched (404), NOT the body chapters. No passage from the chapters is quoted or relied on. The LOC copy is the 1861 printing; the title page shows a copyright entry of 1860, and the work postdates the 1846-47 events discussed in pioneer-supply-chains-failed. Rights: LOC says books in this collection are in the public domain.

sources.title: Trails to Utah and the Pacific diaries and letters, 1846-1869 (Library of Congress American Memory collection)
sources.publisher: Library of Congress, with Harold B. Lee Library (Brigham Young University) and the Utah Academic Library Consortium
sources.supports: Catalogue record for a digitized collection of 49 diaries, 43 maps, 82 photographs and illustrations, and seven published guides for emigrants, about Mormon and other pioneers moving west to Utah, Montana and the Pacific between 1847 and 1869 (collection title runs from 1846).
sources.notes: Upgraded from the register placeholder; the placeholder title 'Pioneer diaries collection' was not the record's actual title. The drafting agent read the catalogue record only, NOT the diaries. The collection is mostly Latter Day Saint migration to Utah and is not a Donner Party source; it is cited only as a place to read ordinary overland provisioning in the travelers' own words.

sources.title: Ways of Catching a Spark: A History of Fire-Making Methods
sources.publisher: Science Museum Group (London)
sources.supports: Museum overview of fire-making: tinder is a fine material that combusts easily; methods fall into percussion, friction, compression of air, chemical, solar and electrical; flint-and-steel is among the oldest and most widespread; friction methods need great skill, fitness and knowledge of conditions; fire pistons (patented in France and England in 1807); Dobereiner's lamp (1823); sulphur splints from China c. 577 AD; John Walker's friction match 1826 (sulfur, antimony sulfide, potassium chlorate, gum; drawn over sandpaper; flaming balls sometimes fell off); white phosphorus (Charles Sauria, 1830) and 'phossy jaw'; 1888 Matchgirl Strikes at Bryant and May; safety matches pioneered by Gustaf Erik Pasch in 1844; ferrocerium (1903) and the lighter.
sources.notes: The page itself says most objects in the collection were acquired by a collector in the late 19th and early 20th centuries and that tracing provenance is difficult and part of a problematic colonial tradition; we repeat that caveat. Dates for the earliest methods are given by the museum as unclear. No image from this page is used.

sources.title: John Walker's Friction Light (A History of the World, object contributed by Preston Hall Museum and Park)
sources.publisher: BBC / British Museum 'A History of the World' project; object contributed by Preston Hall Museum and Park (Stockton Museum Service)
sources.supports: Museum-contributed record of an original friction match (wood, about 9 cm by 0.5 cm). Says Walker, a Stockton-on-Tees chemist, found in 1826 that a chemical-coated stick ignited when scraped on his hearth; first sold on 12 April 1827; early matches were cardboard, then hand-cut wooden splints, later boxed with sandpaper; Walker was advised to patent but did not; Samuel Jones of London launched 'Lucifers' in 1829.
sources.notes: ARCHIVED page ('no longer updated'); content is written by the contributing museum, not the BBC. DISAGREES with Tees Valley Museums on the first sale date (12 April vs 7 April 1827); see hist-field-tvm-walker. Image on the page is credited to Stockton Museum Service and is not used.

sources.title: John Walker and the friction match
sources.publisher: Tees Valley Museums (Preston Park Museum collection)
sources.supports: Walker (born 1781) opened a chemist's shop in Stockton in 1819; made his first friction match by accident in 1826 when a stirring stick scraped against his hearth caught alight; sold his first box on 7 April 1827; did not patent even after advice from Michael Faraday; remained uncredited for decades; a sculpture was unveiled in Stockton in 1977; an original Walker match is in the Preston Park Museum collection.
sources.notes: DISAGREES with the BBC-hosted museum record on the first sale date (7 April vs 12 April 1827). Museum blog post, written by the museum service; used with attribution. Images on the page are credited to Preston Park Museum and are not used.

sources.title: Flint and Steel (Pipe Spring National Monument mystery objects)
sources.publisher: U.S. National Park Service, Pipe Spring National Monument
sources.supports: Park interpretive page: before matches, flint and steel were used for fire; striking steel across flint or other quartz chips off tiny flakes of metal that the action heats until they catch fire; most people carried char cloth, a cloth charred in a fire and smothered, which the sparks ignite and which is then transferred to a tinder bundle and blown into flame; both pioneers and American Indians used flint and steel; steel was a popular trade item.
sources.notes: Short, undated-author interpretive text, last updated 2015. Gives no accuracy or reliability figures. We use it only to describe what the tools were, not as instruction.

sources.title: tinder box (iron), object record DL.376794
sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
sources.supports: Collection record for an iron tinder box classified by the Smithsonian as 'Fire-making and controlling equipment', related to 'Home and Community Life: Domestic Life'; not on view.
sources.notes: Very sparse record: no date, maker, or use description. Cited only to show that tinder boxes are in the national collection under domestic life. The Smithsonian says its database is a work in progress. No image used.

sources.title: Outdoor Fire Safety
sources.publisher: U.S. Fire Administration (FEMA)
sources.supports: Unintentional actions are the leading cause of outside fires; use propane, charcoal and wood-pellet grills only outside (indoor use can cause fire or carbon monoxide poisoning); build campfires at least 25 feet from tents, shrubs and anything that can burn; fire pits, chimneys and outdoor fireplaces at least 10 feet from the home or anything that can burn; watch children at fire pits; use a metal screen over wood-burning fires; put fires out before leaving; store matches and lighters out of children's sight and reach.
sources.notes: Read in full (short page). DISCREPANCY: campfire distance is 25 ft here, 15 ft at NPS, and 10 ft for fire pits at NFPA (NFPA 1 fire code: 50 ft for open fires where adopted, per NFPA's summary). The article reports the range and defers to the local fire authority.

sources.title: Campfires
sources.publisher: U.S. National Park Service
sources.supports: Know the local rules and fire conditions (windy and dry weather may mean campfires are banned) and ask the park before you go; keep tents and flammables at least 15 feet away and upwind; use matches or a lighter on a firestarter; use only lighter fluid as an accelerant and never gasoline; never leave a campfire unattended and keep water nearby; burning anything but wood, especially plastics, can produce toxic gases; douse with plenty of water, and in a pinch stir sand or dirt into spread-out coals; if a fire gets out of control, note your location and call 911.
sources.notes: Read in full. Page last updated 2017-04-17, the oldest of the fire-safety sources. It permits lighter fluid where the park allows; the NFPA article says never to use gasoline or other flammable or combustible liquids. The article follows the stricter statement and names the difference.

sources.title: Wildfire Prevention Tips for Fire Pits and Outdoor Fires (Michele Steinberg, NFPA)
sources.publisher: National Fire Protection Association (nonprofit fire-code and standards developer)
sources.supports: Contact the local fire department about requirements and restrictions before any outdoor fire; some places never allow outdoor fire, others restrict it by season or conditions; avoid burning anything outdoors on windy, dry days because embers can ignite structures or cause a wildfire; supervise outdoor fires; never burn plastics, treated lumber, tires, paint or aerosol containers; never use gasoline or other flammable liquids; fire pits at least 10 feet from anything that can burn; NFPA 1 (where adopted) requires permits and 50 feet from structures for outdoor fires, and an attendant with extinguishing equipment.
sources.notes: NFPA staff article summarizing NFPA educational messages and the NFPA 1 fire code; the article says its opinions are the author's. The drafting agent read the whole article, NOT the NFPA 1 code itself, so the 50-foot and permit statements are reported as NFPA's summary of the code. Kind corrected to 'nonprofit' after the lead's validator change.

sources.title: Carbon Monoxide (CO) Poisoning Basics
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
sources.supports: CO is an odorless, colorless gas that kills without warning; produced when fuel burns in vehicles, small engines, stoves, lanterns, grills, fireplaces, gas ranges and furnaces; symptoms are headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain and confusion, often described as flu-like; people who are sleeping or intoxicated can die before symptoms; never burn charcoal indoors; never use a portable gas camp stove indoors; do not cook or burn anything in a stove or fireplace that is not vented; install battery-operated or battery backup CO detectors near every sleeping area; operate generators only outdoors more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents.
sources.notes: Page was re-dated 2026-10-26, three days before verification. Generator and vehicle-exhaust practices are not reproduced in the article; it links out.

sources.title: Prepare! Don't Let a Winter Storm Take You by Surprise
sources.publisher: NOAA National Weather Service
sources.supports: For winter travel: avoid traveling alone; tell someone your timetable and primary and alternate routes; call 511 for road and weather conditions and restrictions before leaving; carry a Winter Storm Survival Kit whose list includes blankets or sleeping bags, high-calorie non-perishable food, a candle and matches (for light and, in an emergency, heat), a small can and waterproof matches to melt snow, and a compass and road maps, 'don't depend on mobile devices with limited battery life'; more than 5,000 people are killed on average each year in weather-related vehicle crashes.
sources.notes: Page carries no visible update date (page metadata shows 2019 creation). Only the travel-planning and kit-contents statements are used; no quantities are reproduced.

sources.title: What To Do If You're Caught in a Winter Storm
sources.publisher: NOAA National Weather Service
sources.supports: In a vehicle: let someone know where you are going and what route you will take so a search can start in the right place; if the car is stuck, stay in the vehicle because leaving means becoming disoriented quickly in wind-driven snow and cold; be visible to rescuers. The page also gives engine-running and exhaust-pipe instructions to avoid carbon monoxide poisoning, which this archive does not reproduce.
sources.notes: Page carries no visible update date (metadata shows 2019). Contains engine-running timing and a statement that outdoors with no shelter one should 'build a fire for heat'; neither is reproduced or endorsed by this archive. Flagged for the safety reviewer of fire-making-across-time.

sources.title: What made the search for longitude so important?
sources.publisher: Royal Museums Greenwich
sources.supports: Navigational errors and long voyages killed crews; on 22 October 1707 five of Admiral Sir Cloudesley Shovell's ships struck the Isles of Scilly, four sank and more than 1,400 men died, with navigational errors the cause; Spain offered the first longitude reward in 1567 and other states followed; Galileo proposed Jupiter's moons in 1610 and Newton later noted that telescope length and a ship's motion made those eclipses impossible to observe at sea; Longitude Act of 9 July 1714 offered a public reward of 20,000 pounds.
sources.notes: RMG notes there is no evidence of a public outcry after 1707 and that the Act seems to have resulted from lobbying by mathematicians. We keep that nuance.

sources.title: Longitude found - the story of Harrison's timekeepers
sources.publisher: Royal Museums Greenwich
sources.supports: Harrison's H1 (1735) trialled on a 1736 voyage to Lisbon; H4 trialled to Jamaica in 1761 and in the 1763-64 Barbados trial alongside lunar and Jupiter-satellite methods; in February 1765 the Board of Longitude found H4 kept time within the most stringent limits of the 1714 Act, but held back the remainder of the reward until other makers could build similar timekeepers; further testing at the Royal Observatory from 1766 went poorly and the dispute rekindled; marine chronometers were initially very expensive, so roll-out was slow, and cheaper simplified designs allowed wider take-up in the early 1800s.
sources.notes: RMG states that the Harrison family felt the Commissioners had changed the rules; we report both sides as RMG does.

sources.title: Longitude found: Nevil Maskelyne and the lunar method
sources.publisher: Royal Museums Greenwich
sources.supports: Tobias Mayer's lunar tables with a good instrument could, per James Bradley, give a ship's longitude to within 1 degree; the instrument refined in sea trials became the first marine sextant (John Bird); on the 1761 voyage to St Helena Maskelyne found lunars only 1.5 degrees in error against errors of up to 10 degrees from dead reckoning; the calculations were 'decidedly lengthy'; the Nautical Almanac was created to pre-compute lunar data, much of it processed by assistants (computers); marine timekeepers remained rare and expensive; dead reckoning was not abandoned and navigators might use all methods.
sources.notes: These are figures from a single 1761 trial as RMG reports them; they are not a general accuracy claim for later practice.

sources.title: Sextant (Jesse Ramsden, last quarter of the 18th century), Time and Navigation exhibition
sources.publisher: Smithsonian Institution (National Museum of American History object; Time and Navigation exhibition, National Air and Space Museum)
sources.supports: Exhibition record for a sextant made by Jesse Ramsden in the last quarter of the 18th century; the sextant became the symbol of navigation; the instrument is named for its scale of 60 degrees, one sixth of a circle, and can measure larger angles than the octant.
sources.notes: Short caption-level record. No image used (Smithsonian credit lines apply).

sources.title: What is declination?
sources.publisher: U.S. Geological Survey
sources.supports: At most places a compass does not point exactly to geographic north; the deviation is called declination; it has been a nuisance to navigators for centuries and varies with both location and time; at very high latitudes a compass can even point south; the collar of USGS topographic maps shows the magnetic declination at the map center in the year the map was made; NOAA offers a calculator for any location and date.
sources.notes: Page was fetched in full; the output was large and only the explanatory text was read.

sources.title: What do the different north arrows on a USGS topographic map mean?
sources.publisher: U.S. Geological Survey
sources.supports: A diagram at the bottom of most USGS topographic maps shows true north, grid north and magnetic north and the angles between them; some maps, especially very old ones, do not have it; true north is the direction of the line of longitude bisecting the quadrangle; magnetic north on the map is the direction a magnetic compass would point at the time the map was published, and it varies over time and with position.
sources.notes: Only the opening explanation was read closely; the rest of the large page (related links) was skimmed.

sources.title: Magnetic Declination
sources.publisher: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information
sources.supports: Declination is the angle between magnetic north and true north, positive east and negative west; it changes over time and with location; a compass points along the horizontal component of the local magnetic field, not at any single point such as the magnetic pole; true bearing is magnetic bearing plus declination when west is negative; NOAA provides calculators and the World Magnetic Model.
sources.notes: Does not state the size of declination anywhere in the US; we do not either.

sources.title: What is the North Star and How Do You Find It?
sources.publisher: NASA Science (Preston Dyches, public engagement specialist)
sources.supports: Polaris is not the brightest star but is usually easy to spot; it sits close to, not exactly at, the north celestial pole and traces a very small circle, so it stays in roughly the same place and is a reliable way to find the direction of north in the Northern Hemisphere (true north, not magnetic); the two pointer stars at the end of the Big Dipper's cup point to Polaris; the Southern Hemisphere has no bright star marking the south celestial pole and observers there can use other ways, including the Southern Cross; the pole star changes over thousands of years because of a roughly 26,000-year wobble.
sources.notes: The page gives no numerical accuracy for using Polaris as a direction guide. We state none.

sources.title: Donner and Reed Wagon Train Incident
sources.publisher: U.S. National Park Service, California National Historic Trail
sources.supports: Lansford W. Hastings claimed a timesaving route (the Hastings Cutoff) through the Great Salt Lake Desert; late starters found it enticing; the Donner-Reed party of 87 people left Illinois on April 12 and passed Independence, Missouri on May 12 with 2,500 miles to go, joining Hastings' group of 80 wagons to save 150-500 miles (Hastings 'a little vague'); the route took more time than the popular routes, depleting supplies and livestock; they reached the Humboldt River on September 26 and Truckee Lake in October, exhausted and low on provisions, and were trapped by snow for four months; once the animals were killed by mid-December they ate rawhide; some left on a self-rescue mission and resorted to cannibalism; 40 of the 87 died of starvation-related causes; survivors were not rescued until spring 1847. Quotes Sarah Winnemucca that her Paiute people 'would have helped' but were afraid.
sources.notes: DISCREPANCIES with other sources: NPS counts 87 people and 40 deaths; McCurdy (1994) counts 90 people and 42 deaths; Britannica says Donners and Reeds left Springfield April 14 and gives 42 deaths and 47 survivors; the Utah state history essay says 47 of 87 reached Sutter's Fort. The NPS page also gives the departure from Illinois as April 12. The saving Hastings claimed is stated as 150-500 miles by NPS and 'more than 300 miles' by Britannica. Read in full (short page). Kind 'museum' is the closest fit for an NPS interpretive history page; flagged.

sources.title: The Hastings Cutoff (Thomas G. Alexander, from Utah, The Right Place)
sources.publisher: Utah Division of State History (History to Go)
sources.supports: Hastings published his Emigrants Guide to Oregon and California in 1845; it is unclear whether he meant to promote the cutoff from Fort Bridger or only to say that a more direct route than via Fort Hall was possible; Fremont, Hudspeth, Bridger and Vasquez favored the cutoff, while James Clyman tried to dissuade the Donner-Reed party and Joseph R. Walker thought it an unproven risk; four parties took the cutoff in 1846; the Donner-Reed party left Fort Bridger on July 31, found a note from Hastings warning against Weber Canyon and promising a better road, and took the Emigration Canyon route, losing more time and meeting extreme hardship there and in the Salt Lake Desert; 'only forty-seven of the original eighty-seven reached Sutter's Fort'.
sources.notes: A state-agency history essay by a professional historian; short and without footnotes. Its '47 of 87' implies 40 deaths, matching NPS but not McCurdy or Britannica.

sources.title: Epidemiology of disaster. The Donner Party (1846-1847) (S A McCurdy), Western Journal of Medicine 160(4):338-342
sources.publisher: Western Journal of Medicine, via PubMed Central (author at UC Davis School of Medicine)
sources.supports: Abstract: the party consisted of 90 persons, median age 19.5 years (range 1 to 70), 55 (61%) male, 72 (80%) traveling with family; 42 (47%) died; age was the most important mortality risk factor, with lowest mortality (10%) at ages 6 to 14 and highest for children under 6 and adults 35 and over; persons traveling without family had about twice the relative risk, as did men and boys; the author suggests that keeping family structures intact may improve survival in nutritionally stressed populations.
sources.notes: The drafting agent read the abstract and bibliographic record only; the full text is scanned page images and was NOT read. The 90-person count differs from NPS and Utah's 87; the abstract does not explain the difference. A commentary, 'Previous Donner Party research', exists in volume 161, p. 92, and was not read.

sources.title: Donner Memorial State Park
sources.publisher: California State Parks
sources.supports: The park's Visitor Center has exhibits on the Emigrant Experience, the Donner Party, the Land of the Washoe, Chinese construction of the railroad, and early motoring over Donner Pass; the Pioneer Monument, completed June 6, 1918 by the Native Sons of the Golden West (California Historical Landmark #134), stands on a 22-foot pedestal where the Schallenberger and later the Breen cabin once stood; restored in 2022; park lies near an elevation of about 6,000 feet; the park contains the alignment of the primary Emigrant Trail in Coldstream Canyon.
sources.notes: A visitor-information page, not a history narrative: it gives no account of the party's deaths or supplies. Used only for the memorial, the location, and the fact that interpretation covers Indigenous peoples of the area. The plaque wording often quoted online was NOT verified here and is not used.

sources.title: Donner party (Encyclopaedia Britannica)
sources.publisher: Encyclopaedia Britannica (editors; most recently revised by Michael Ray)
sources.supports: Tertiary reference summary: Hastings Cutoff was proposed by an unreliable guide and was in reality 125 miles longer than the established trail; Reed was warned at Fort Laramie by a friend who had just come east through the cutoff; the party spent about two weeks breaking a trail through the Wasatch; a note from Hastings said the Great Salt Lake Desert could be crossed in two days but it took five; dozens of cattle were lost and several wagons abandoned; Paiute warriors killed several remaining oxen; they cached nearly all personal possessions except food, clothing and essentials; snow blocked the pass on October 31; many oxen wandered off and were lost in the snow; deaths totaled 42 with 47 survivors; Breen's diary is the only contemporary written record of the ordeal; in 2010 researchers reported no physical evidence of cannibalism at Alder Creek while noting absence of evidence does not rule it out.
sources.notes: Tertiary encyclopedia article; the register's kind list has no 'reference' kind, so 'scholarship' is the closest available and is imperfect (flagged for the lead). Read in full. Used for specific figures that NPS and the Utah essay do not give (the desert crossing, the 125-mile figure, relief-party dates), each attributed by name in the text. Its figure of 42 deaths with 47 survivors does not add up to the 87-person party it names. Britannica attributes oxen losses to Paiute warriors, whereas NPS quotes Sarah Winnemucca that her people were afraid and would have helped; the article reports the disagreement.

sources.title: Patrick Breen Diary, 1846 November 20 - 1847 March 1 (BANC MSS C-E 176), finding aid
sources.publisher: The Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley, via the Online Archive of California
sources.supports: Finding aid for the manuscript diary kept by Patrick Breen at Donner (Truckee) Lake from November 20, 1846 to March 1, 1847: a 32-page booklet with entries on the first 29 pages; terse, matter-of-fact style recording weather, health, food, deaths and visits; ends on the day Reed's relief party arrived; the diary passed from Breen to George McKinstry to H. H. Bancroft; early printed versions (from a May 1847 newspaper copy) are considered corrupt through omissions, alterations or falsification; Teggart (1910) is the first complete scholarly edition and Stewart (1946) added a transcription and facsimile.
sources.notes: Read in full (finding aid prose). The diary's own entries, the digital images and the container-listing transcription were NOT read. The finding aid's background paragraph repeats the standard account (starvation; some survivors consumed the dead) without citing sources. It does not say this is the only contemporary record. Finding aid dated 1997 (source date March 2011).

sources.title: The emigrants' guide to Oregon and California (Lansford W. Hastings, Cincinnati, 1845), Internet Archive scan, full text
sources.publisher: Internet Archive (scan of the 1845 Cincinnati edition; holding library not verified)
sources.supports: Primary source. In the passages read (OCR of printed pages around 137-139): the entire distance "by this route" from Independence "either to Oregon or California" is about "twenty-one hundred miles" and the usual time about 120 days exclusive of delays, though parties had often taken longer; emigrants had so far traveled together as far as Fort Hall, the only settlement in that vicinity where they could obtain horses and provisions, but the guide names the Soda Springs, not Fort Hall, as the point where the routes would most advantageously diverge; a California route is described leaving the Oregon route and heading southwest toward the Salt Lake.
sources.notes: The drafting agent fetched the full OCR text (about 540,000 characters) but READ ONLY the passages around the California-route summary (printed pp. ~137-139) and the Bear River valley passage; the rest was not read. The OCR is noisy and the Salt Lake passage is too garbled to quote or characterize with confidence, so no claim is made about what the guide recommends for the cutoff. The details page (archive.org/details/GR_1815) was not itself opened; the URL came from a search result and the text from /stream/GR_1815/GR_1815_djvu.txt. Other copies exist (BYU Trail Guides, HathiTrust) and were not checked. CORRECTED 2026-11-02 after an independent review: an earlier version of this record and of the article said the distance and time were 'by the Fort Hall route'. The guide's words are 'by this route', in a passage that names the Soda Springs, not Fort Hall, as the best point for the routes to diverge; the distance is printed in words ('twenty-one hundred miles') in the OCR (read again on 2026-11-02 from /stream/GR_1815/GR_1815_djvu.txt, around character 590,000 of the cleaned text).
